Definition: Whether the civil registration and digital ID systems are integrated
Comments: Civil registration documents (birth certificates, residential cards) are required to obtain a national ID card, indicating a degree of linkage. However, civil registration is incomplete (less than 40% of births registered per UNICEF), decentralized, and not digitally integrated with the ID system. Score=1 for partial/procedural linkage only.

Definition: Whether the digital ID credential serves as legal proof of an individual's identity as codified in law
Comments: The national ID card is recognised as the primary legal proof of identity and citizenship in Eritrea. It is required to obtain a passport and access government services. Citizens over 18 are required to hold one. The ID card is compulsory and serves as legal proof of identity.

Definition: Whether formal legislation (act, law, regulation) governs digital identity including identification acts, digital ID laws, or equivalent legislation
Comments: The issuance of national ID cards is governed by Proclamation No. 21/1992 (promulgated 6 April 1992). This provides a basic legal framework for the national ID card. However, it does not address digital identity, data protection, or modern ID management. No updated identity law has been enacted. Score=1 for a basic legal basis only.

Definition: Whether the system and the production of credentials can be managed, maintained and developed by in-country technical staff (as opposed to foreign vendors)
Comments: The Department of Immigration and Nationality (under the Ministry of Internal Affairs) is responsible for issuing and maintaining the national ID system. Institutional capacity is severely constrained by the exodus of qualified personnel, limited infrastructure, and restricted digital connectivity. No dedicated digital ID maintenance unit has been documented. Score=1 for basic government maintenance.

Definition: Whether the ongoing management, maintenance and development of the ID system can be funded by sustainable domestic resources
Comments: Fees are charged for ID cards (100 nakfa in Eritrea; $25-$100 in diaspora). The system has operated since 1992 indicating basic sustainability. However, the new electronic card rollout was extremely slow (~70,000 issued by 2016), suggesting severe financial and logistical constraints. No international donor support for the ID system has been documented. Score=1 for basic fee-supported operation.

Definition: Whether the system collects biometric data and which modalities are collected (fingerprints, facial image, iris scans)
Comments: The new electronic national ID card (rolled out from 2014/2015) includes a fingerprint on the back of the card. Applicants provide one fingerprint at time of application. However, only approximately 70,000 new cards were issued by 2016 from a population of ~3.5M; the vast majority still hold old handwritten cards with no biometrics. Score=1 reflects limited/partial biometric collection.

Definition: Whether identity records are stored in electronic/digital format versus paper-based records
Comments: EASO (2015) references 'a print-out from the electronic population register' as a document used for civil status issuance, suggesting some electronic records exist at the Department of Immigration and Nationality. However, the system is largely paper-based and fragmented; no central national biometric database has been documented. Score=1 for partial/basic electronic records.

Definition: Whether the country has established or is actively developing a national digital identity system, including foundational ID systems that enable authentication across multiple services. Fully deployed means operational nationwide and accepting new registrations.
Comments: Eritrea has a national identity card system established by Proclamation No. 21/1992. A new electronic card with fingerprint and holographic features was introduced in 2014/2015, but very few are in circulation (approx. 70,000 by 2016). No digital ID platform in the modern sense exists (no unique digital identifier, no digital authentication infrastructure). Score=1 reflects existence of a basic national ID with limited electronic features.

Definition: Whether credentials are issued free of charge
Comments: A fee of 100 nakfa (approximately $6-8 USD) is charged for a new ID card in Eritrea. Diaspora applicants pay $25 (new) to $100 (replacement) in US dollars. Fees are non-refundable. The in-country fee represents a cost barrier given Eritrea's severe poverty levels. Score=1 for fee-based (not free, but relatively modest in-country fee).

Definition: Whether registration for digital ID is mandatory, optional, or mandatory for specific groups
Comments: The national ID card is compulsory for all Eritrean citizens aged 18 and above. It is required to access government services and obtain a passport. However, enforcement is inconsistent particularly in rural areas and among diaspora. Certain groups (Jehovah's Witnesses, deserters) are actively denied the ID. Score=2 for mandatory with uneven enforcement.

Definition: Percentage of eligible population that has been issued or registered with digital ID credentials
Comments: The old handwritten ID card is nominally held by adults (18+) but coverage is incomplete especially in rural areas and among ethnic minorities. Only ~70,000 new electronic cards had been issued by 2016 from a population of ~3.5M. Jehovah's Witnesses and some minorities are systematically denied ID cards. Birth registration rate below 40% affects future ID eligibility. Score=2 for partial coverage.

Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for registering for social assistance programs and accessing social services
Comments: The national ID card is referenced for access to government administrative services and food coupon distribution in urban areas. However, there is no formal social protection system or social registry. Access to limited state services requires the ID card, but cards are denied to certain groups (Jehovah's Witnesses, military deserters). Score=1 for informal/limited use.
